title: Semantic Layer
shortDefinition: A metadata layer that translates business terminology into database queries for AI analytics tools.
definition: A semantic layer is a metadata layer that translates between business terminology and underlying database structures — defining what business concepts like 'revenue,' 'active customer,' and 'churn rate' mean in terms of specific database tables, columns, and calculation logic, so AI-powered analytics tools and LLMs can answer business questions in natural language without requiring users to know underlying database schemas. The semantic layer is increasingly the critical piece that determines whether 'text-to-SQL' and natural language analytics tools actually work reliably for business users or consistently fail on queries outside simple examples.

sections.title: Why the semantic layer is the key to reliable text-to-SQL
sections.description: A semantic layer encodes business logic that LLMs can't infer from raw database schemas alone.

content.text: The dream of letting business users ask data questions in plain English sounds simple — ask 'what was last quarter's revenue by region?' and get a chart. The practical challenge is that LLMs asked to generate SQL directly against raw database schemas frequently produce incorrect queries, because business logic is embedded in analyst knowledge rather than the schema itself: 'revenue' might require joining three tables with specific filtering logic that no LLM would infer from schema names alone. A semantic layer explicitly encodes this business logic — what 'revenue' means, how 'active customer' is defined, what the correct date logic for 'last quarter' is in your system — giving the LLM a business-vocabulary interface rather than raw schema, dramatically improving query correctness.

items: Raw schemas — LLMs can't infer business logic from table names.
Business logic — encoded in analyst knowledge, not the database.
Semantic layer — explicitly defines metrics and calculations.
Business vocabulary — LLM queries using business terms, not schema.
Correctness improvement — dramatically more reliable than raw schema access.

sections.title: Semantic layers vs. knowledge graphs vs. RAG

content.text: These concepts address related but distinct problems. A knowledge graph represents entity relationships (company A owns company B, product X is in category Y). A RAG system retrieves relevant documents for question answering. A semantic layer specifically addresses the translation between business terminology and database query logic — it's the piece that makes AI-powered SQL generation and structured data analytics reliable rather than a parlor trick that works on simple queries and fails on real business questions.

content.title: Complementary technologies
content.text: These concepts can work together — a semantic layer for structured data, RAG for documents, and a knowledge graph for entity relationships.

sections.title: Limitations and risks of semantic layers

content.text: Semantic layers have limitations. They require upfront investment to encode business logic. The layer must be maintained as business definitions and database schemas evolve. Complex business logic may be difficult to encode completely. The semantic layer alone doesn't guarantee correct SQL generation — LLM quality and prompt design still matter. The layer may not handle all business questions, especially those involving complex multi-domain queries. Organizations may underestimate the maintenance effort required to keep the semantic layer accurate.

faqs.title: Frequently asked questions about semantic layers

items.question: What's an example of business logic a semantic layer encodes?
items.answer: Defining 'active customer' as 'a customer with at least one order in the last 90 days and account status = active' — logic an analyst knows intuitively but that a raw database schema doesn't express, and that an LLM can't reliably infer from table and column names alone.

items.question: Can a semantic layer be built on top of any database?
items.answer: Yes, semantic layers are typically database-agnostic, translating business logic into queries appropriate for your specific database system.

items.question: Does a semantic layer require existing BI tools, or can it work independently?
items.answer: A semantic layer can serve LLM-powered analytics directly or integrate with existing BI tools — ClickMasters designs the architecture based on your existing analytics infrastructure.

items.question: How long does building a semantic layer take?
items.answer: 10–28 weeks depending on business domain complexity and whether a natural language analytics interface is included.

items.question: Does a semantic layer need to be maintained as our business logic changes?
items.answer: Yes — as business definitions and database schemas evolve, the semantic layer needs to be updated to stay accurate; ClickMasters designs semantic layers for maintainability and includes documentation for ongoing governance.

items.question: Is a semantic layer different from a data catalog?
items.answer: Related but distinct — a data catalog inventories available data assets with metadata; a semantic layer specifically encodes the business logic and calculation definitions needed to translate business questions into correct queries.

items.question: What is the relationship between a semantic layer and text-to-SQL?
items.answer: A semantic layer is the key enabler for reliable text-to-SQL. It provides the business logic and metric definitions that allow LLMs to generate correct SQL queries rather than guessing from raw schema names.

items.question: Can a semantic layer be built incrementally?
items.answer: Yes — it's often practical to start with the most frequently used business metrics and domains, then expand coverage over time as the system proves its value.

items.question: What is the difference between a semantic layer and a metric store?
items.answer: A semantic layer is broader — it includes business logic for metrics, dimensions, and entity relationships. A metric store specifically focuses on storing and serving defined metrics. They are related and often used together.

items.question: How does a semantic layer improve LLM-generated SQL?
items.answer: By providing the LLM with a business-vocabulary interface and explicit metric definitions, rather than raw database schemas. This reduces the ambiguity and inference burden on the LLM, resulting in much more accurate SQL generation.
